passages.title: Urban Trees and Public Health
passages.instruction: Questions 1-13. Choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
text: City planners have recently renewed interest in planting trees as part of urban health policy. Earlier approaches viewed trees mainly as decorative elements, but a larger body of evidence now links green streets to measurable health outcomes. Residents in areas with higher tree coverage often report lower stress, reduced noise irritation, and greater willingness to walk for short journeys.

One reason is microclimate control. Tree canopies reduce direct sunlight on roads and pavements, limiting the urban heat island effect. During summer, this can lower local temperatures by several degrees. Cooler streets can encourage outdoor activity, especially among children and older people who avoid heat exposure.

Trees can also influence air quality. Leaves and bark trap some particulate matter from traffic, although the effect varies by species and street design. In narrow streets with heavy congestion, poorly placed dense planting may slow air circulation. For this reason, urban foresters increasingly choose mixed species and spacing strategies rather than uniform rows.

However, practical barriers remain. Maintenance costs are significant over the long term. Young trees require irrigation and protection, while mature trees can damage pavements or underground utilities if roots are unmanaged. Municipal budgets often prioritize short-term infrastructure projects that produce visible results within election cycles.

Despite these challenges, several cities have adopted tree equity programs. These programs map neighborhoods by income, existing canopy, and health risk indicators. Funding is then directed toward districts with the least tree cover and highest vulnerability to heat and respiratory illness. Early evaluations suggest that targeted planting can narrow environmental health gaps between wealthier and poorer districts.

Experts caution that trees are not a complete solution. They work best alongside safer cycling routes, reduced vehicle emissions, and better building design. Still, as one urban health researcher noted, trees are unusual because they provide multiple benefits at once: cooling, shade, visual relief, and social value.

passages.title: How Sleep Supports Learning
passages.instruction: Questions 14-26. Choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
text: For many years, students were advised to treat sleep as optional during exam periods. Recent neuroscience research has challenged that belief. Sleep is now understood as an active biological process that helps stabilize memory and regulate attention.

During waking study sessions, the brain encodes new information in temporary patterns of neural activity. During sleep, particularly non-rapid eye movement stages, these patterns are replayed and gradually integrated with existing knowledge. This process is often called consolidation.

Researchers have tested this in controlled experiments. Participants who learned word lists and then slept generally recalled more items than participants who remained awake for an equivalent interval. Similar effects have been found in motor learning tasks, such as finger-sequence practice.

Sleep also helps selective memory. Not every detail is retained equally. Information judged as important, emotionally meaningful, or expected to be tested tends to receive stronger consolidation. In educational settings, this suggests that clear learning goals may influence what the sleeping brain prioritizes.

However, duration alone does not explain outcomes. Fragmented sleep with repeated awakenings can weaken consolidation even if total hours appear adequate. Consistent sleep timing also matters, since irregular schedules may disrupt circadian rhythms and reduce next-day alertness.

Some students attempt to compensate by extending sleep at weekends. While partial recovery is possible, it does not fully reverse weekday deficits in concentration or mood. Experts therefore recommend regular sleep patterns across the week.

Short daytime naps can provide limited benefits. A nap of around 20 to 30 minutes may improve alertness and reduce fatigue, while longer naps can produce sleep inertia, a temporary period of grogginess after waking. Naps are best viewed as supplements, not substitutes for nighttime sleep.

Educational institutions are beginning to respond. Universities have introduced workshops on sleep literacy, and some schools are experimenting with later start times. Early evidence suggests improvements in attendance and self-reported wellbeing, though long-term academic effects are still being studied.

passages.title: Tracking Plastic in the Oceans
passages.instruction: Questions 27-40. Choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.
text: Ocean plastic pollution is often discussed through dramatic images of floating debris. Yet scientists emphasize that visible waste is only one part of the problem. A substantial proportion of marine plastic exists as fragments too small to be seen easily from ships or coastlines.

To estimate distribution, researchers combine surface net sampling, satellite drift models, and shoreline surveys. No single method is complete. Nets can miss particles below mesh size, while shoreline counts are influenced by tides, local cleanup efforts, and tourism patterns.

One challenge is the movement of plastic across regions. Items released in one country can travel long distances through currents before beaching elsewhere. This complicates legal responsibility and often creates tension between coastal communities and upstream producers.

Scientists also distinguish between primary and secondary microplastics. Primary microplastics are manufactured at small sizes, such as some industrial pellets. Secondary microplastics result from larger objects degrading through sunlight, wave action, and mechanical abrasion.

Potential ecological impacts include ingestion by fish, seabirds, and plankton-feeding organisms. Ingestion can reduce feeding efficiency and expose animals to associated chemicals. However, researchers caution that risk levels vary by species, habitat, and concentration.

Policy responses increasingly target prevention rather than cleanup alone. Extended producer responsibility schemes require manufacturers to share waste-management costs. Deposit-return systems can improve collection rates for beverage containers. Some cities have also restricted certain single-use items.

Technological innovation contributes but is not a stand-alone solution. Biodegradable materials may perform differently across environments and can still require specific disposal conditions. Advanced sorting systems can improve recycling streams but depend on stable funding and public participation.

Most experts argue that long-term progress depends on coordinated action across product design, consumer behavior, and infrastructure. Monitoring remains critical: without consistent data, it is difficult to evaluate whether interventions genuinely reduce marine plastic loads.
